summary: Return the n-th term of the sequence that starts at "1" and where each term is the run-length encoding of the previous one.
mainInsight: Nothing clever: start from "1" and apply run-length encoding n - 1 times. The only care point is grouping maximal runs and flushing the final run.
invariant: While scanning a term, every run before index i has already been written as count followed by digit.

approaches.name: Iterative run-length encoding
approaches.summary: Loop n - 1 times; scan the current string, count each run of equal digits, append count + digit.
approaches.spaceComplexity: O(L_n), the length of the answer

approaches.name: Recursion
approaches.spaceComplexity: O(L_n + n) with the call stack
approaches.interviewRelevance: Fine, but mention the iterative version.

personalSolution.approach: Iterative run-length encoding, building each term with temp += str(count) + res[i]
personalSolution.timeComplexity: O(sum of term lengths) in CPython; += on a str can be quadratic in other runtimes
personalSolution.notes: Same algorithm as the canonical code. Appending pieces to a list and joining once guarantees linear time per round; CPython often optimises temp += in place, but you should not rely on it in an interview.

canonicalCode:
class Solution:
    def countAndSay(self, n: int) -> str:
        s = "1"
        for _ in range(n - 1):                 # n - 1 encoding rounds
            out = []
            i = 0
            while i < len(s):                  # one linear scan of the current term
                j = i
                while j < len(s) and s[j] == s[i]:
                    j += 1                     # j stops at the end of the run
                out.append(str(j - i))         # count
                out.append(s[i])               # digit
                i = j
            s = "".join(out)                   # list + join avoids quadratic string concatenation
        return s
commonMistakes: Forgetting to append the final run after the scan loop (when the loop only emits on a digit change).
Writing digit then count instead of count then digit.
Building the string with += inside the scan (quadratic in some languages).
edgeCases: n = 1 returns "1" without any encoding round.
Long runs of three equal digits ('111' -> '31').

promptVariants: In your solution, why does the inner loop compare res[i] with res[i + 1], and why is there an i += 1 after appending?
Walk through how this loop finds each run and moves to the next one.
cards.answer: The inner while extends the run while the next character equals the current one, leaving i on the last character of the run, with count holding its length. After writing count + digit, i += 1 steps onto the first character of the next run. The i + 1 < len(res) guard stops the look-ahead at the end, so the last run is written without a separate flush.
keyPoints: Inner loop stops with i on the run's last character
i += 1 moves to the next run
Look-ahead guard means no final flush needed
cards.explanation: Look-ahead scanning writes each run as soon as it ends, which avoids the classic forgot-the-last-run bug.
cards.code:
res = "1"
for _ in range(n - 1):
    temp, i = "", 0
    while i < len(res):
        count = 1
        while i + 1 < len(res) and res[i] == res[i + 1]:
            i += 1
            count += 1
        temp += str(count) + res[i]
        i += 1
    res = temp
return res

promptVariants: Derive the running time of the canonical code in terms of the term lengths.
How much work does the whole loop do, and how fast do the terms grow?
cards.answer: Round k scans the current term once, so total work is the sum of the term lengths L_1 + ... + L_(n-1) (plus building L_n). Terms grow by roughly 30% per step (Conway's constant, about 1.30), so the cost is exponential in n, but linear in the size of the output being built.
keyPoints: Lengths grow geometrically (~1.3x), so exponential in n
cards.explanation: The inner while loops only advance i and j forward, so each round is linear in the current term length.
